evidence.claim: Lake Willoughby’s cliff views lead into the Passumpsic River valley.
evidence.quote: These overlooks provide views of the lake's clear waters and the cliffs that rise on either side.

evidence.claim: the Passumpsic River valley
evidence.quote: Lyndon is located in the valley of the Passumpsic River in northeastern Vermont.

evidence.claim: The Northeast Kingdom drive follows Lake Willoughby’s eastern shore on VT 5A, with overlooks facing the water and cliffs on either side.
evidence.quote: Vermont Route 5A features several scenic overlooks along the eastern shore of Lake Willoughby, including at the Devil's Rock and Mount Pisgah pull-offs. These overlooks provide views of the lake's clear waters and the cliffs that rise on either side.

evidence.claim: Farther south, US 5 follows the Passumpsic River between Lyndon and St. Johnsbury.
evidence.quote: US 5 continues north along the Passumpsic River from St. Johnsbury for about 7.5 miles (12.1 km) until it reaches the town of Lyndon.

evidence.claim: VT 5A passes through Willoughby State Forest, where Mount Pisgah stands east of the lake and Mount Hor to the west.
evidence.quote: Willoughby State Forest is easily accessible from State Routes 5 and 5A and is bisected by Lake Willoughby, with Mount Hor (2648 feet) to the west and Mount Pisgah (2751 feet) to the east.

evidence.claim: The lake road began its numbered life as New England Interstate Route 2A, an alternate to Route 2 in the regional road-marking system of 1922–1927.
evidence.quote: The entirety of modern VT 5A was first designated as New England Interstate Route 2A (NEI 2A), part of the New England road marking system that existed between 1922 and 1927.

evidence.claim: an alternate to Route 2
evidence.quote: NEI 2A was designated as an alternate to NEI 2

evidence.claim: Route 2 became US 5, while the alternate became a state highway.
evidence.quote: NEI 2 was designated as US 5 in 1926 and NEI 2A was redesignated as a state highway.

evidence.claim: Vermont took responsibility for US 5 in 1931 and finished paving it in 1933.
evidence.quote: The state of Vermont started paving the route in 1931, and it was completed by 1933.

evidence.claim: Vermont took responsibility for US 5 in 1931
evidence.quote: US 5 was not maintained by the state of Vermont until the creation of the state highway system in 1931.

evidence.claim: The lake route’s number changed, but its course and role as the easterly alternative between Burke and Derby remained.
evidence.quote: While the designation of VT 5A has changed since its initial construction, its routing and function have not.

evidence.claim: the easterly alternative between Burke and Derby
evidence.quote: Both routes connect Burke with Derby, but VT 5A uses a more direct, easterly route than US 5.

evidence.claim: Begin at Newport on Lake Memphremagog and head through Derby Center toward Charleston.
evidence.quote: In Newport, US 5 picks up a five-mile-long (8.0 km) concurrency with VT 105 that takes US 5 across I-91 and into the village of Derby Center.

evidence.claim: Begin at Newport on Lake Memphremagog
evidence.quote: The city surrounds the southern shore of Lake Memphremagog.

evidence.claim: VT 5A shares VT 105 between Derby Center and Charleston before continuing to Lake Willoughby and West Burke.
evidence.quote: VT 5A continues along a silent concurrency with VT 105 from Charleston to Derby Center.

evidence.claim: before continuing to Lake Willoughby and West Burke.
evidence.quote: VT 5A proceeds north into Orleans County and the town of Westmore traversing through the Willoughby State Forest and along the eastern side of Lake Willoughby

evidence.claim: At West Burke it meets US 5; continue south toward Lyndon and St. Johnsbury.
evidence.quote: West Burke is located 8 miles (13 km) north of the village of Lyndonville along U.S. Route 5. Vermont Route 5A intersects US 5 in the center of the village, leading north to Lake Willoughby.

evidence.claim: At St. Johnsbury, the Passumpsic meets the Moose and Sleeper’s rivers, placing the southern end of the drive at another meeting of waterways.
evidence.quote: Situated at the confluence of the Passumpsic, Moose and Sleeper's rivers

evidence.claim: Newport occupies the southern shore of Lake Memphremagog, where the Clyde, Barton and Black rivers enter the lake.
evidence.quote: The city surrounds the southern shore of Lake Memphremagog. Three of the four major rivers in the county empty into the lake here: the Clyde, Barton, and the Black.

evidence.claim: Railroad construction reached the settlement in 1863, and Lake Bridge incorporated as the Village of Newport five years later.
evidence.quote: The railroad was constructed to Newport in 1863.  In 1868, the Lake Bridge settlement was incorporated as the Village of Newport.

evidence.claim: The Lady of the Lake began carrying passengers in 1867 and operated until 1917.
evidence.quote: The Lady of the Lake steam excursion/ferry boat started operating in 1867. It stopped operations in 1917.

evidence.claim: The city uses the steamboat as its logo, preserving a visible link to that era of lake travel.
evidence.quote: This steamboat is used as Newport's logo.

evidence.claim: The railway’s connections to outside markets helped the village expand. Passenger service later declined as people turned to cars; Newport’s last passenger train left in 1965.
evidence.quote: The small village expanded because of increased connections to outside markets and ease of transportation; it attracted more residents. By the late 20th century, railroad passenger traffic had declined because people relied on individual vehicles; the last passenger train left Newport in 1965.

evidence.claim: A painted devil faces the lake from Devil’s Rock on the Mount Pisgah shore.
evidence.quote: It takes its name from a painted image of a devil on the front of the rock facing out toward the lake.

evidence.claim: on the Mount Pisgah shore.
evidence.quote: Devil's Rock, located on the Mount Pisgah side of the lake

evidence.claim: The VT 5A pull-off offers views across the water toward the cliffs.
evidence.quote: Vermont Route 5A features several scenic overlooks along the eastern shore of Lake Willoughby, including at the Devil's Rock and Mount Pisgah pull-offs. These overlooks provide views of the lake's clear waters and the cliffs that rise on either side.

evidence.claim: Lake Willoughby exceeds 300 feet in depth in places, and its depth makes its surface freeze later than other Northeast Kingdom lakes.
evidence.quote: Willoughby is over 300 feet (91 m) deep in places

evidence.claim: its depth makes its surface freeze later than other Northeast Kingdom lakes.
evidence.quote: Because of its depth, the surface of the lake freezes later than other lakes in the Northeast Kingdom.

evidence.claim: Mount Pisgah and Mount Hor’s sheer cliffs support arctic and cliff-alpine plants and provide nesting habitat for peregrine falcons.
evidence.quote: The sheer cliffs of Mount Pisgah and Mount Hor provide an environment conducive for arctic and cliff-alpine plants, as well as ideal nesting areas for the rare peregrine falcon.

evidence.claim: Tourists once traveled this water by small steamboat. Those boats operated from 1884 into the early 1900s, when gasoline engines replaced steam power.
evidence.quote: Tiny steam boats operated on the lake for tourists from 1884 to the early 1900s when steam was replaced by the gasoline engine.

evidence.claim: The east-shore overlooks face Lake Willoughby and the cliffs rising on both sides.
evidence.quote: These overlooks provide views of the lake's clear waters and the cliffs that rise on either side.

evidence.claim: The Passumpsic River powered Lyndon’s gristmills and sawmills, but the railroad shifted its business center.
evidence.quote: The Passumpsic River, flowing through the center of the town, provided power for grist and saw mills.

evidence.claim: About 1867, the Connecticut & Passumpsic Rivers Railroad bypassed Lyndon Corner and Lyndon Center, drawing business to Lyndonville.
evidence.quote: About 1867, the Connecticut & Passumpsic Rivers Railroad bypassed Lyndon Corner and Lyndon Center. This resulted in business moving to Lyndonville.

evidence.claim: Covered bridges record another part of the town’s transport history.
evidence.quote: The Old Schoolhouse Bridge is a historic covered bridge spanning the South Wheelock Branch of the Passumpsic River in Lyndon, Vermont.

evidence.claim: The Old Schoolhouse Bridge dates to 1871 and spans the South Wheelock Branch of the Passumpsic.
evidence.quote: Built in 1871, it is one five similar bridges in Lyndon.

evidence.claim: Its trusses have vertical board siding inside as well as outside, an unusual detail among Lyndon’s bridges.
evidence.quote: It is one of five bridges in Lyndon, the only one to have its interior clad in siding.

evidence.claim: The bridge stands south of the modern road crossing, with a metal gabled roof extending beyond its timber trusses.
evidence.quote: The covered bridge is located just south of the modern bridge carrying that road. It is a single-span king post truss, 42 feet (13 m) in length. It is covered by a gabled metal roof, which extends beyond the trusses.
